title: Mirabai
hook: a holy man in Vrindavan won't meet a woman, and Mira sends him one sentence

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai with bells on her ankles, dancing while the town called her mad, and wearing the word as her own.

A door, and a message passed through it. On one side, a learned renunciant in Vrindavan who has made a rule for himself: he doesn't meet women. On the other, a woman who has walked a long way to see him, and has just been turned away. She doesn't argue about the rule. She sends back a single sentence, and by the end of the story, the door opens. The woman is Mira, and the sentence is today's whole lesson.
screen: `A DOOR, AND A MESSAGE.` → `A RULE: NO WOMEN.` → `ONE SENTENCE BACK.`

segments.voice: First, where she is. Tradition says that after the troubles with her husband's family, Mira left the palace and took to the road, and came to Vrindavan, the country of Krishna's childhood, where the cowherd girls, the gopis, once ran to the sound of his flute. Holy people and teachers lived there. The story names one of them as Jiva Goswami, a scholar of Krishna devotion; some tellings name another teacher. The story, in paraphrase: Mira asks to meet him. Word comes back that he has vowed not to see women. And Mira answers, roughly: I thought there was only one man in Vrindavan, Krishna. I didn't know anyone else here was claiming to be a man. The renunciant hears it, and comes out to meet her. It's sharp, and it's funny. But under the wit is a teaching that belongs to Vrindavan itself. In the devotion Vrindavan is known for, the soul stands before Krishna the way the gopis did: as the beloved, waiting for him. Before him, no one is the man of the house. So the rule that kept her out rested on a difference that, in that place, she says doesn't count. And she doesn't attack his vow, or his learning, or him. She takes the faith of the place more seriously than the rule does, and lets that speak. Last, this isn't a record anyone wrote down at the door. It's one of the stories told about her, remembered because it teaches, the way a parable does.
screen: `MIRA COMES TO VRINDAVAN` · `A HOLY MAN WHO WON'T MEET WOMEN` · `ONLY ONE MAN IN VRINDAVAN` · `A STORY THAT TEACHES`

segments.voice: Notice the labels you carry today: your job, your role at home, how others see you. Name one quietly, then on an out-breath set it down beside you like a bag, and for a few breaths just be someone breathing, without a title. If you pray, you can stand before God for a moment without it.
Mirabai. Turned away in Vrindavan by a holy man who wouldn't meet women, she answered that there was only one man there, Krishna.
Your line: Mirabai. She answered a closed door with the faith of the place. That's day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Vrindavan remains a place of pilgrimage for Krishna devotees, and stories of Mira's time there are told alongside her songs in bhajan gatherings.

sources.ref: Hagiographical tradition of Mirabai: the meeting at Vrindavan (often told of Jiva Goswami)

notes: The Vrindavan meeting is told as tradition. Most tellings name Jiva Goswami; some name Rupa Goswami or another teacher. The script says 'some tellings name another teacher'; confirm.
Confirm the paraphrase of Mira's reply (that she thought Krishna was the only purusha in Vrindavan and all others gopis).
Chronology (whether Mira and Jiva Goswami could have met) is deliberately not discussed; a Keeper may want a note.
Gaudiya Vaishnava sensitivity: the story should not read as a put-down of Jiva Goswami; the script frames it as her answering from the faith of the place without attacking him. Check tone.
Original game uses Vrindavan (वृन्दावन) rather than Mira's name, since day 1356 used मीराबाई.
